Growing Elsewhere: Ghorbatī (غربتی) is an evolving installation that investigates the condition of living as ghorbatī (غربتی)—a Persian word describing someone who exists away from home, outside belonging, or in a state of estrangement. Through large-scale charcoal drawings on unstretched muslin, suspended textile scrolls, ceramic elements, and performance, the project considers transplantation as both a biological process and a metaphor for migration. Borrowing the logic of transplanting plants and organs, the work explores how displaced bodies are expected to adapt to unfamiliar environments while remaining vulnerable to rejection.

Marriage for Survival is an installation accompanied by a performance that revisits rituals of the Iranian wedding ceremony through the experiences of femininity, expectation, and belonging. In the traditional ceremony, unmarried young women hold a gauze cloth above the couple while grinding sugar cones together, a gesture believed to bring sweetness and fortune to the marriage. Drawing from my own memories of participating in these rituals, I re-stage the gesture without a bride or groom. I grind the sugar for myself, transforming a ritual traditionally performed in service of a union into an act of questioning and refusal. As sugar crystals pass through the gauze and dissolve on the ground, the ritual loses its promise of sweetness and becomes a meditation on the roles and futures prescribed to women. Through this altered ceremony, I consider how identity, belonging, and the idea of a “complete” self can be shaped by social expectations and external structures—and what it might mean to reclaim that space for oneself.
